title: Art Dealers in the US
one_liner: US art dealers are recovering unevenly as high-end auctions rebound, art fairs regain share and online-only sales cool from pandemic highs.
overview: Art Dealers in the US includes galleries and auction houses that retail original and limited-edition artworks, often by buying inventory for resale, selling on consignment or arranging auctions for a commission. The 2022 IBIS baseline showed a fragmented, mature industry with $11.4 billion in revenue, 21,452 establishments, 21,217 enterprises, 33,762 employees and a 9.1% profit margin. Current 2025 market data show the broader US art market returned to growth after two declining years: US art-market sales reached $26.0 billion in 2025, up 5% year over year, while US dealers posted aggregate sales growth of 2%. The recovery is led more by high-end auction activity and proven blue-chip material than by speculative contemporary demand.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 broader US art-market sales: $26.0B; 2025 implied US dealer/gallery channel: about $15.3B if the US 44% global share is applied to 2025 global dealer sales of $34.8B
key_stats.growth: 2025 US art-market sales growth: +5% year over year; 2025 US dealer aggregate sales growth: +2% year over year; 2025 global dealer sales growth: +2% year over year
key_stats.global_market: 2025 global art-market sales: $59.6B, up 4% year over year
key_stats.global_dealer_sales: 2025 global dealer-sector sales: $34.8B, up 2% year over year
key_stats.global_public_auction_sales: 2025 global public auction sales: $20.7B, up 9% year over year
key_stats.online_sales: 2025 global online art and antiques sales: $9.2B, equal to 15% of total market sales, down 3 percentage points year over year
key_stats.art_fairs: 2025 art fair sales: 35% of dealer turnover, up 4 percentage points year over year
key_stats.profitability_pressure: 2025 dealer operating costs rose about 5% on average, above aggregate dealer sales growth

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 IBIS revenue growth: +3.8%; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: -1.3%; projected 2022-2027 revenue CAGR: +1.8% to $12.4B
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 IBIS product mix: paintings 38.0%, prints 20.9%, drawings 19.9%, other media 9.8%, sculptures 7.6%, photography 3.8%

how_it_makes_money: Dealers earn revenue by reselling owned inventory, taking commissions on consigned works, brokering private sales, running auctions, charging buyer and seller premiums, staging fairs and exhibitions, and providing related advisory, valuation, financing and collection-management services. Galleries typically rely on primary-market representation and private sales, while auction houses generate fee income from public auctions, private sales and financial services secured by art.
cost_structure: Major costs are artwork purchases and consignor payouts, gallery and saleroom rent in expensive art districts, specialist wages, cataloging and provenance research, insurance, storage, shipping, art-fair booths, marketing, digital platforms, legal compliance and finance costs. The 2025 environment is margin-sensitive because dealer operating costs rose about 5% on average while aggregate global dealer sales rose only 2%.
current_dynamics: The 2025 market is improving but selective. US sales are growing again, high-end New York auctions regained momentum and all top 10 global lots in 2025 sold in New York, but dealer performance is mixed: 43% of US dealers reported improved 2025 sales while 37% reported declines. Buyers are favoring quality, provenance, major estates and established artists, while younger and speculative contemporary segments remain weaker. Online-only sales remain important for entry-level and new buyers but have lost share as high-value transactions move back to fairs, galleries and live salerooms.
whats_growing: Blue-chip and historically validated art, major single-owner collections, New York high-end auctions, art fairs, lower-end dealer segments under $500,000 turnover, female artist representation, new-buyer acquisition at small dealers and hybrid sales models that combine physical fairs with digital lead generation.
whats_shrinking: Online-only market share, weaker speculative contemporary and young contemporary demand, sub-$50,000 public auction sales, dealer profitability for operators unable to absorb higher rent, staffing, insurance and fair costs, and smaller galleries without strong collector relationships or distinctive artist programs.
recent_developments: 2025: US art-market sales rose 5% year over year to $26.0B, keeping the US at 44% of global art sales by value.
2025: Global art-market sales rose 4% year over year to $59.6B after two years of declines.
2025: Global dealer sales rose 2% year over year to $34.8B, while dealer operating costs rose about 5% on average.
2025: Online art and antiques sales fell to $9.2B, or 15% of total market sales, the lowest level since 2019.
2025: Christie's projected $6.2B in global sales, up 6% year over year, including $4.7B in auction sales.
2026: Dealer sentiment improved, with 43% expecting 2026 sales to improve and 38% expecting stable sales.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously positive. Wealth concentration, lower-rate expectations, estate consignments and resumed in-person buying should support large auction houses and top-tier galleries. Growth for the broader dealer base will likely be slower because operating costs, art-fair expenses, tariffs, shipping and insurance remain high. Dealers with strong artist access, provenance expertise, private-client relationships and omnichannel sales infrastructure are best positioned; undifferentiated small galleries remain exposed to rent pressure and inconsistent discretionary spending.

title: Artificial Grass Turf Installation
one_liner: Artificial grass turf installers convert sports fields, homes and commercial landscapes to synthetic surfaces, benefiting from water-saving demand but facing tougher PFAS, heat and end-of-life scrutiny.
overview: Artificial Grass Turf Installation is a construction services niche made up of contractors and vertically integrated turf suppliers that prepare sites, install base layers and drainage, lay synthetic turf, add infill and maintain or replace fields and lawns. The 2021 baseline defined the industry as installation-only, excluding manufacturing, and placed 2020 revenue at $2.645 billion with a 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 2.6% to about $3.0 billion in 2025. Current 2025-2026 conditions are mixed: athletic and soccer demand is strong, California-style water conservation supports replacements of nonfunctional grass, and public construction remains sizable, but residential construction is interest-rate sensitive and schools, cities and universities are asking harder questions about PFAS, heat, microplastics and disposal.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $3.0 billion in U.S. artificial grass turf installation revenue based on the baseline 2020-2025 forecast; 2025 U.S. artificial turf product-market revenue was separately estimated at $1.163 billion by Grand View Research.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025: 2.6% CAGR in the baseline installation forecast; 2026-2033: 8.3% CAGR forecast for the U.S. artificial turf product market by Grand View Research.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2020: 7.7% baseline industry profit margin; 2025: 7.9% baseline forecast profit margin.
key_stats.establishments: 2020: 1,720 establishments in the baseline report; 2025: 1,855 enterprise forecast in the baseline outlook.
key_stats.employment: 2020: 12,042 workers in the baseline report; 2025: 13,389 workers in the baseline outlook.
key_stats.demand_mix: 2020: fields and sports applications were 62.0% of revenue, nonresidential artificial grass installation was 19.0%, residential artificial grass installation was 10.5%, and other public/commercial uses were 8.5%.
key_stats.construction_indicator: May 2026: U.S. construction spending was $2.210 trillion at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, 1.5% below May 2025; private residential construction was $930.2 billion and private nonresidential construction was $738.7 billion.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: approximately $2.78 billion, calculated from the baseline 2020 revenue of $2.645 billion using the baseline 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 2.6%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: approximately 2.6% annual growth implied by the baseline 2020-2025 forecast CAGR.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2022: approximately 7.8%, interpolated between the baseline 2020 margin of 7.7% and 2025 forecast margin of 7.9%.
baseline_2022.note: 2022 values are baseline-derived estimates because the source file provided 2020 actuals and a 2025 forecast, not a separate 2022 table.

how_it_makes_money: Installers earn project revenue from site assessment, demolition or grass removal, grading, drainage and aggregate-base work, turf procurement markup, installation labor, infill, seams, edge restraints, striping, maintenance, repair and replacement. In 2020, the baseline revenue mix was led by sports fields and playgrounds at 62.0%, followed by nonresidential landscaping at 19.0%, residential lawns at 10.5% and other public/commercial uses at 8.5%. Larger players also make money through bundled design-build, manufacturer-certified installation, multi-field school contracts and recurring maintenance agreements.

cost_structure.labor: 2020: wages were $697 million, equal to about 26.4% of 2020 revenue in the baseline file.
cost_structure.purchases: 2025-2026: turf rolls, infill, shock pads, drainage materials, adhesives, edging and rental equipment remain the largest direct project costs; vertically integrated suppliers reduce purchase-cost exposure by combining manufacturing, distribution and installation.
cost_structure.profit: 2020: baseline profit was $204 million, or 7.7% of revenue; 2025: baseline forecast margin was 7.9%.
cost_structure.other_costs: 2025-2026: insurance, bonding, fuel, disposal, compliance testing, warranty reserves and subcontracted excavation/drainage work are material overhead items, especially for school and municipal athletic-field projects.
cost_structure.risk_costs: 2026: PFAS testing, cooler infill specifications, stormwater controls and recycling or landfill fees are becoming more common bid requirements for public-sector projects.

current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. On the positive side, sports participation, soccer growth ahead of the 2026 World Cup, school athletic upgrades and commercial water-saving projects support installations and field replacements. On the negative side, higher financing costs, softer 2026 construction spending versus 2025, environmental objections and public procurement scrutiny slow some projects. Buyers increasingly specify no intentionally added PFAS, lower surface temperatures, better drainage, organic or alternative infill, shock attenuation and end-of-life recycling documentation.
whats_growing: 2025-2026: soccer and multiuse athletic fields, helped by record U.S. soccer participation and school sports participation.
2025-2026: replacement fields with upgraded pads, drainage, cooling infill and documented PFAS-free components.
2025-2026: drought-prone commercial and institutional landscaping where owners want lower irrigation and maintenance costs.
2026: public and private projects that can document compliance with ASTM F3782-26 PFAS sampling/testing practices.
2026-2033: U.S. artificial turf product-market revenue, forecast by Grand View Research to grow at an 8.3% CAGR.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026: projects using crumb rubber or older infill specifications where schools or municipalities face heat, chemical or microplastic concerns.
2025-2026: discretionary residential installations in markets pressured by interest rates and weaker housing turnover.
2026: bidders without PFAS documentation, recycling plans or third-party performance testing.
2026: low-bid public projects that cannot absorb higher material, testing and disposal costs.
2025-2026: natural-grass-to-turf conversions in jurisdictions where local moratoria or environmental review requirements delay approvals.
recent_developments: 2025: Grand View Research estimated U.S. artificial turf product-market revenue at $1.163 billion and projected an 8.3% CAGR for 2026-2033.
September 2025: NFHS reported 8,266,244 high school sports participants for 2024-25, a record and up 203,942 from 2023-24.
March 2026: SFIA reported that 250 million Americans participated in at least one sport, fitness or leisure activity in 2025.
May 2026: ASTM F3782-26 was published to standardize sampling and testing of synthetic turf fiber and fabric for PFAS.
May 2026: U.S. Census reported construction spending at a $2.210 trillion annual rate, 1.5% below May 2025 but with private residential construction at $930.2 billion.
July 2026: SFIA reported outdoor soccer participation reached 16.8 million in 2025, an all-time high ahead of the 2026 World Cup.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is moderately positive but more compliance-heavy than the 2021 baseline implied. Sports-field replacement cycles, soccer participation, public-school athletics and water conservation should keep demand growing, while slower construction, public opposition and environmental rules make growth uneven by region. Installers with school and municipal references, PFAS documentation, cooler surface systems, drainage expertise and recycling partnerships should gain share. Smaller local contractors can still win residential and commercial landscaping jobs, but larger vertically integrated suppliers are better positioned for multi-field public and institutional contracts.
one_sentence: The industry installs synthetic turf systems for athletic fields, playgrounds, residential lawns, commercial properties and public spaces, with 2025 demand supported by sports participation and drought-resilient landscaping while 2026 purchasing decisions increasingly require PFAS documentation, cooler infill and recycling plans.

title: Arts, Entertainment and Recreation in the US
one_liner: A broad discretionary-experience sector spanning live events, sports, museums, amusement parks, casinos, fitness and other recreation venues.
overview: NAICS 71 operators sell in-person and hybrid leisure experiences to consumers, tourists, sponsors and public or nonprofit funders. The sector includes performing arts and spectator sports, museums and historical sites, amusement and theme parks, gambling, fitness, golf, marinas, bowling, arcades and other recreation services. Demand is discretionary, so revenue tracks disposable income, consumer confidence, travel volumes, leisure time and event calendars. After the 2020 shock and 2021-2022 reopening rebound, 2025 growth normalized: Census QSS all-establishment revenue totaled $439.1 billion in 2025, up 5.3% from 2024, while Q1 2026 revenue of $103.5 billion was up 4.1% from Q1 2025. BEA value added reached $355.8 billion in 2025, up 8.9% from 2024, confirming that the sector has regained economic weight even as some subsectors face labor, insurance, rent, artist guarantees and weather-related cost pressure.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: $439.1 billion revenue, based on U.S. Census QSS quarterly NAICS 71 all-establishment revenue summed across 2025.
key_stats.growth: 2025: +5.3% revenue growth vs 2024; Q1 2026 revenue was $103.5 billion, +4.1% vs Q1 2025.
key_stats.value_added: 2025: $355.8 billion BEA GDP/value added for NAICS 71, up 8.9% from 2024.
key_stats.employment: June 2026: 2.69 million seasonally adjusted payroll jobs in BLS NAICS 71; 2025 occupational employment included 298,210 amusement and recreation attendants and 219,050 fitness trainers.
key_stats.establishments: Q4 2025: 194,192 private establishments in BLS QCEW NAICS 71, plus 5,905 government establishments.
key_stats.wages: May 2026: average hourly earnings were $30.27 for all employees and $24.37 for production and nonsupervisory employees in NAICS 71.
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline: IBISWorld estimated profit of $26.4 billion and a 7.1% EBIT margin; current margins vary widely by venue ownership, event guarantees, labor intensity and real estate costs.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $372.0 billion revenue in 2022 dollars in the IBISWorld baseline file.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: +24.0% revenue growth, with 2017-2022 revenue CAGR of +1.5% after the 2020 pandemic decline.
baseline_2022.profit: 2022: $26.4 billion profit, equal to a 7.1% margin.
baseline_2022.employment: 2022: 5.07 million workers in the IBISWorld baseline file.
baseline_2022.establishments: 2022: 1.92 million establishments and 1.90 million enterprises in the IBISWorld baseline file.
baseline_2022.wages: 2022: $130.3 billion total wages in the IBISWorld baseline file.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from admissions, memberships, event tickets, concessions, venue rental, sponsorships, media and naming-rights packages, gaming win, merchandise, lessons and classes, tours, parking, premium seating, digital ticketing fees and public or philanthropic support for cultural institutions. Large venues and franchises monetize attendance through higher-yield ancillary spending, while artists, promoters and smaller recreation businesses depend more directly on ticket sales, bookings, subscriptions and local repeat customers.
cost_structure: The sector is labor- and facility-intensive. Key 2022 baseline costs included wages of $130.3 billion, about 35.0% of IBISWorld revenue, and profit of $26.4 billion, or a 7.1% margin. Major cost buckets include wages and benefits, performer or team compensation, artist guarantees, gaming taxes, rent and real estate, utilities, insurance, maintenance, security, marketing, ticketing and payment fees, food and beverage inputs, depreciation on attractions and venues, and debt service. In 2026, BLS reported NAICS 71 average hourly earnings of $30.27 in May, keeping labor availability and wage inflation central margin issues.
current_dynamics: The strongest current demand is in live entertainment, commercial gaming, sports betting, premium experiences and destination recreation. Live Nation reported 2025 revenue of $25.2 billion, up 9%, and 65 million fans at operated venues, up 8%, showing that consumers are still paying for concerts and festivals. Commercial gaming hit a 2025 record of about $78.7 billion in gross gaming revenue, helped by sports betting and iGaming. National parks remained resilient with 323.0 million recreation visits in 2025, though visits declined 2.7% from 2024. Theme parks and museums continue to depend on domestic leisure travel and international tourism, while local recreation operators are more exposed to household budgets, rent, insurance and weather disruptions.
whats_growing: Sports betting, iGaming, premium seating, concert touring, festivals, sponsorship, food and beverage upsell, destination theme-park spending, fitness and wellness formats, immersive attractions, dynamic pricing, mobile ticketing and data-driven yield management are growing. The commercial gaming vertical is especially strong: 2025 sports betting revenue rose 22.8% and iGaming revenue rose 27.6%, according to the American Gaming Association. BEA NAICS 71 value added grew 8.9% in 2025, faster than headline GDP growth.
whats_shrinking: Pandemic-rebound tailwinds are fading, so growth is slowing from reopening-era spikes. National Park Service recreation visits fell 2.7% in 2025 from the 2024 record. Some legacy local recreation formats, including bowling centers, golf courses, marinas and lower-margin family entertainment venues, remain vulnerable to real estate costs, maintenance capex and aging customer bases. Museums and nonprofit cultural institutions face uneven attendance recovery, donor competition and public-funding uncertainty. Price-sensitive consumers are trading down on concessions, memberships and discretionary outings when ticket, travel and lodging costs rise together.
recent_developments: 2025: Census QSS NAICS 71 revenue totaled $439.1 billion, up 5.3% from 2024.
2025: BEA reported NAICS 71 GDP/value added of $355.8 billion, up 8.9% from 2024.
February 2026: AGA reported 2025 U.S. commercial gaming revenue of $78.7 billion, up 9.2%, with sports betting up 22.8% and iGaming up 27.6%.
March 2026: National Park Service reported 323.0 million recreation visits in 2025, down 2.7% from 2024, with 26 parks setting records.
June 2026: BLS reported NAICS 71 payroll employment of 2.69 million jobs and Q4 2025 private establishments of 194,192.
Q1 2026: Census QSS revenue for NAICS 71 reached $103.5 billion, up 4.1% from Q1 2025.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but less explosive than the 2021-2023 reopening phase. Revenue should keep growing as event calendars, casino demand, sports betting, premium experiences and domestic leisure spending expand, but the sector is exposed to consumer fatigue from higher prices and to cost pressure from labor, insurance, rent, security and capital projects. Operators with owned venues, strong brands, recurring memberships, digital distribution, sponsorship inventory and pricing power should outperform. Smaller venues, nonprofit arts organizations and weather-dependent attractions face narrower margins and more volatile attendance.
themes: Tourism recovery and domestic travel dependence
Weather and climate exposure for outdoor recreation

title: Audio & Video Equipment Distributors
one_liner: A mature wholesale channel for TVs, cameras, audio systems and related AV gear, pressured by direct-to-retailer sourcing and e-commerce but supported by premium displays, smart-home integration and professional AV demand.
overview: The industry remains in structural decline as a pure consumer-electronics wholesaling channel: cameras, physical media players and standalone audio products keep losing share to smartphones, streaming and multifunction devices, while large retailers and online marketplaces increasingly buy directly from manufacturers. The 2025-2026 backdrop is mixed rather than uniformly negative. Consumer technology spending stabilized after the 2022-2024 correction, TVs and portable audio were forecast to contribute to 2025 gains, and larger-screen TV refresh cycles support dollar sales even as unit pricing remains competitive. The healthier pockets are professional AV, digital signage, security-adjacent video, smart-home automation and integrator channels, where distributors can bundle inventory, financing, design help, installation support, software and proprietary brands. The weakest pocket is commodity household electronics sold through retailers that can bypass wholesalers.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated market size: $45B-$46B for U.S. audio and video equipment distributors, benchmarked to the public January 2025 IBISWorld/R&M figure of $45.1B in 2023 and a stabilized 2025 consumer-tech demand backdrop.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated industry growth: roughly 0% to +2%; Circana forecast U.S. consumer technology sales revenue to grow 1.6% in 2025, while CTA forecast total U.S. consumer technology retail revenue at $537B in 2025, up 3.2% year over year.
key_stats.profitability: 2025-2026 profitability remains thin for broadline wholesalers, but specialty AV/security distributors can exceed the old industry average; ADI disclosed 2025 gross margin of 22.3% and standalone adjusted EBITDA margin of 6.2%.
key_stats.demand_indicators: 2025 real disposable personal income increased 1.7%; May 2026 private residential construction was $930.2B SAAR; May 2026 housing starts were 1.177M SAAR, down 8.7% from May 2025.
key_stats.channel_pressure: 2026 Circana forecast U.S. consumer technology sales revenue of $112B, up only 0.2%, after projected second-half 2025 sales declined 2.2% year over year.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated market size: $46.2B, derived from the January 2025 IBISWorld/R&M public excerpt reporting 2023 revenue of $45.1B after a 2.4% decline.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 growth: not disclosed in the public 2025 excerpt; baseline trend indicates a post-2021 rebound plateau before the 2023 decline of 2.4%.
baseline_2022.context: The older baseline file reported 2021 revenue of $35.8B, 2021 growth of 6.9%, 2021 profit margin of 2.0%, and a pre-2026 forecast of $37.5B by 2026, but the January 2025 update revised the series materially higher to $45.1B in 2023.

how_it_makes_money: Distributors earn a spread between bulk purchase costs and resale prices, plus fees or margin lift from freight, inventory availability, credit terms, vendor rebates, private-label or exclusive brands, configuration services, installation support, project design, training, warranties and software-enabled remote management for integrators.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost bucket; the 2021 baseline described the model as bulk purchasing from manufacturers and reselling at a small markup, and 2025 tariff volatility keeps product costs exposed.
cost_structure.wages: Moderate cost for sales teams, warehouse labor, technical support, category specialists and project-design staff; the 2021 baseline reported $1.1B in wages.
cost_structure.freight_and_warehousing: Material cost because large TVs, displays, speakers and AV racks are bulky, damage-prone and often time-sensitive for retail resets or installation projects.
cost_structure.technology_and_ecommerce: Rising spend on digital ordering, inventory visibility, pricing tools, ERP integration, vendor portals and remote-support platforms.
cost_structure.profit: Low for commodity wholesale; higher for specialty distributors with exclusive brands, software, value-added services and project support.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Commodity consumer AV distribution is still squeezed by Amazon, big-box direct sourcing, manufacturer direct sales and weak demand for cameras and disc players. Specialty channels are healthier because integrators need a single distributor for smart-home control, commercial displays, collaboration rooms, security video, data networking and post-sale support. Tariffs and sourcing shifts are also changing buying behavior: CTA warned in 2025 that tariff actions could reduce purchasing power for consumer tech products by up to $123B annually if passed through, while PIIE reported that 2025 China-origin imports of laptops/monitors and game consoles fell sharply even as total imports stayed roughly flat through sourcing shifts to countries such as Vietnam.
whats_growing: 2025 larger-screen TV refresh demand and portable audio sales, which Circana said would help drive 2025 consumer-tech gains.
2025-2026 professional AV: direct-view LED, digital signage, collaboration rooms, healthcare, education, enterprise and live-event installations.
2025-2026 smart-home and residential integration: control, lighting, networking, security video and remote-management software.
2025-2026 exclusive/private-label brands, where ADI disclosed 2025 exclusive-brand revenue of more than $800M and gross margin roughly 3x third-party product sales.
2025-2026 security-adjacent video and data communications, especially when bundled with AV and low-voltage installation work.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 standalone cameras for casual users as smartphones substitute for point-and-shoot photography and video.
2025-2026 DVD, CD, Blu-ray and other physical-media playback devices as streaming remains dominant.
2025-2026 small independent consumer electronics retailers that depend on wholesalers but face online and big-box price competition.
2025-2026 commodity TV and audio distribution margins when large retailers buy directly from manufacturers.
2025-2026 China-centered sourcing for tariff-exposed consumer electronics, with distributors managing vendor lead-time and cost volatility.
recent_developments: 2025-01: Circana forecast U.S. consumer technology sales revenue to grow 1.6% in 2025, adding $1.8B, with computers, portable audio and TVs contributing more than 70% of gains.
2025-05: CTA said current and announced tariff actions could reduce U.S. consumer purchasing power by up to $123B annually across ten everyday tech product categories if fully passed through.
2025-07: Resideo announced plans to separate ADI Global Distribution into an independent public company focused on low-voltage products including security and audio-visual solutions.
2026-01: CTA projected U.S. consumer technology retail revenue would reach $565B in 2026, up 3.7% year over year despite tariffs and economic pressure.
2026-01: Circana forecast U.S. consumer technology sales revenue at $112B in 2026, up 0.2%, after a challenged second half of 2025.
2026-06: ADI disclosed 2025 revenue of $4.8B, 2025 gross margin of 22.3%, and 2025 AV at about 30% of revenue in spin-off filings.
outlook: Expect low growth with continued consolidation. The 2026 demand setup is not a broad consumer-electronics boom: Circana sees only 0.2% U.S. consumer technology retail growth in 2026, and housing starts in May 2026 were below May 2025. Still, the industry can grow in value-added niches where distributors solve complexity for integrators: commercial AV, security video, smart-home control, digital signage, networking and exclusive brands. Operators without specialty services, digital ordering scale, vendor breadth or working-capital discipline will keep losing share to manufacturers, marketplaces and large retailers.
one_sentence: Audio & Video Equipment Distributors buy household-type audio and visual equipment in bulk from manufacturers and resell it to electronics retailers, mass merchants, e-commerce sellers, integrators and specialty resellers, earning thin wholesale margins on product availability, brand breadth, logistics and channel support.

title: Audio & Video Equipment Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature, import-heavy US manufacturing niche that survives on premium audio, automotive infotainment, pro sound and connected-home hardware rather than mass-market TVs and legacy media devices.
overview: This industry manufactures electronic audio and video equipment used in home entertainment, vehicles, public venues, studios and commercial sound systems, including speakers, amplifiers, headphones, soundbars, receivers, infotainment audio components and video hardware. The 2025 industry is no longer a broad US mass-production base for consumer electronics; it is a smaller, more specialized manufacturing and design ecosystem built around premium sound, automotive OEM programs, professional audio, connected-home devices and selective domestic assembly. Public BLS sectoral output reached $4.393 billion in 2025, only 0.3% above 2024 and 4.8% below 2022, while Census M3 shipments totaled $5.465 billion in 2025, down 4.6% from 2024. The gap between resilient end-market spending and weak domestic manufacturing volume reflects the sector's core tension: US consumers keep buying audio/video technology, but a large share of physical production remains offshore.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling finished audio/video equipment and components to consumer electronics retailers, e-commerce channels, automakers, commercial integrators, theaters, venues, enterprise buyers and distributors. Higher-margin revenue comes from premium speakers, soundbars, headphones, microphones, installed audio, cinema/commercial systems, vehicle audio programs, branded accessories and replacement or upgrade cycles tied to larger screens, streaming, gaming, connected homes and in-car infotainment.
cost_structure: The industry's 2025 cost base is dominated by electronic components, semiconductors, circuit boards, plastics, metals, magnets, glass, packaging, freight, tariffs and contract manufacturing costs. Labor is smaller than in less automated manufacturing but remains important for engineering, product design, quality control, final assembly and pro-audio production; the 2022 baseline reported $630 million of wages in 2021. Profitability depends on component pricing, offshore sourcing, freight rates, retailer bargaining power, warranty costs, R&D spending and the ability to command premium pricing for differentiated audio performance or vehicle-integration contracts.
major_players: Gentex Corporation / VOXX / Premium Audio Company
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Consumer technology demand remains large, with CTA projecting $537 billion of US consumer technology revenue in 2025 and $565 billion in 2026, but domestic audio/video manufacturing is flatter because production is global and replacement demand for traditional devices is mature. Tariffs became a larger cost issue in 2025, with CTA estimating consumer technology importers paid $23.5 billion in tariffs in 2025 and the average industry tariff rate rose from 1% to 7% by the end of 2025. Producer prices for domestic audio/video equipment rose into 2026, while 2026 shipments through June ran below 2025 levels. Automotive audio, premium home audio, commercial sound, creator tools and spatial/noise-canceling headphones are healthier than legacy DVD players, low-end TVs and commodity consumer electronics assembly.
whats_growing: Premium audio, spatial audio, active noise cancellation, Bluetooth and wireless speakers, creator and podcast microphones, conferencing audio, installed commercial sound, cinema audio, connected-home audio, vehicle infotainment audio and branded high-performance home theater products are growing or defending price better in 2025-2026. Automotive OEM and aftermarket channels are especially important because audio/video equipment is increasingly embedded in digital cockpits, driver displays and differentiated vehicle interiors.
whats_shrinking: Legacy DVD/Blu-ray hardware, standalone MP3 players, commodity TVs, low-end speakers, undifferentiated receivers and mass-market domestic assembly are shrinking in relevance. Smartphone, tablet, smart-TV and streaming-platform substitution continues to reduce the need for separate audio/video devices, while high import penetration keeps pressure on US establishments that cannot compete on labor, scale or component sourcing.
recent_developments: January 2025: CTA projected US consumer technology revenue of $537 billion in 2025, up 3.2% from 2024, while warning tariffs could reduce purchasing power by $90 billion-$143 billion.
April 2025: Gentex closed its VOXX acquisition, adding Klipsch, Onkyo, Integra and other premium audio brands and expecting $325 million-$375 million of annual revenue contribution.
2025: BLS reported NAICS 334310 sectoral output of $4.393 billion, up 0.3% from $4.381 billion in 2024 but below $4.615 billion in 2022.
2025: Census M3 audio and video equipment shipments totaled $5.465 billion, down 4.6% from $5.731 billion in 2024.
May 2026: CTA reported consumer technology importers paid $23.5 billion in tariffs in 2025, more than five times the $4.0 billion paid in 2024.
June 2026: The audio/video equipment manufacturing PPI was 107.858, up from 102.860 in December 2024, signaling higher domestic producer prices.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautious. Sectoral output held roughly flat in 2025, but Census shipments in January-June 2026 were 9.0% below the same 2025 period, implying pressure from tariff pass-through, slower hardware unit growth and mature replacement cycles. Over 2026-2028, the strongest operators should be those with premium brands, automotive OEM relationships, professional/commercial channels, software-connected features and flexible sourcing. Domestic reshoring is likely to be selective rather than broad, focused on high-value audio, final assembly, quality-sensitive production and supply-chain risk reduction rather than low-margin commodity electronics.
